name: Anchor mastopexy

lead: Anchor mastopexy is a breast-lift operation using an anchor-shaped (inverted-T) incision pattern: around the areola, vertically down, and along the breast fold. It lets the surgeon remove the most skin and raise the nipple-areola complex, giving a higher and more compact breast shape.
It is generally used for moderate to severe sagging after pregnancy, weight loss or ageing. Scars fade but stay visible, and the final shape can take about a year to settle.[1]

paras: The procedure is done by a plastic surgeon under anaesthesia. Skin is removed, breast tissue reshaped and the nipple moved to a higher position. A surgical bra and support tape are used during healing, with follow-up visits in the first weeks.[1]

Reported risks include bleeding, infection, nipple or skin necrosis, fluid collections, wound separation, temporary or lasting change in nipple sensation, asymmetry and contour irregularities. Smoking, diabetes, obesity and aspirin use are linked to higher nipple-necrosis risk. The inframammary scar is prone to thickening.[1]

chain: Excess skin removed through inverted-T incisions
Nipple-areola complex and tissue repositioned higher
angle.text: The operation changes breast position and skin envelope directly. Patients seek it for sagging after pregnancy, weight loss or ageing, trading the extra scarring of the anchor pattern for greater skin removal.

lead: Anchor mastopexy, also called the inverted-T, Wise-pattern or Lexer-pattern breast lift, is a surgical technique that raises sagging breasts by removing excess skin, reshaping breast tissue and moving the nipple-areola complex higher.[1] In looks terms it is a hardmaxxing procedure aimed at breast position and shape.

It uses three incisions, around the areola, vertically from the areola to the breast crease, and along the inframammary fold, which gives the surgeon the widest skin removal. It is therefore the pattern generally associated with severe ptosis (sagging).[1]

Published surgical literature on breast lifts is largely made up of technique descriptions and case series, and a scar-healing gel trial in women having breast reduction or mastopexy is registered.[2][3]

paras: Sagging is commonly attributed to gravity, pregnancy and breastfeeding, weight loss, menopause and ageing, which stretch the skin and weaken the Cooper's ligaments. Surgeons often grade ptosis with the Regnault scale (I to IV) based on nipple position relative to the inframammary fold. Mild cases may be treated with an implant alone, while moderate to severe ptosis usually calls for a lift.[1]

The anchor pattern is the most extensive option. Milder cases may use the periareolar (Benelli), circumvertical (lollipop) or Regnault B patterns, which leave fewer scars but allow less skin removal. The nipple's blood supply is kept through a pedicle (superior, inferior or medial) chosen by how far it must move. Lift and implant can be combined, with higher complication rates than either alone.[1]

Support tape is typically removed after 7 to 10 days, a surgical bra is worn, and the surgeon usually reviews the patient weekly for the first three weeks. Final shape may take about a year to settle.[1]
The anchor pattern leaves three scars. The one along the fold is the most prone to thickening. Scars fade with time but remain visible.[1]

General risks are bleeding, infection and anaesthesia effects. Specific ones are skin or nipple necrosis, seroma, haematoma, wound dehiscence, altered nipple sensation (usually temporary), asymmetry and contour irregularities. Aspirin use, smoking, diabetes and obesity are linked with nipple necrosis. Scars may complicate breast self-exam and imaging.[1]

A 2003 case series of 117 patients described a different, subareolar mastopexy technique and its modifications; it concerns that technique rather than the anchor pattern.[2] A clinical trial registered in 2025 (CHITOSCAR, 39 participants, not yet recruiting) plans to test a scar-healing gel in women undergoing breast reduction or mastopexy.[3]
